lesson.title: Kubernetes control plane scheduling and reconciliation
lesson.why: A saved manifest is only a request. Locating the component that cannot advance that request prevents random restarts and unnecessary cluster changes.
lesson.what: Follow a Pod from API admission through scheduling, node execution, and repeated reconciliation. Separate desired configuration from observed status.

concepts.name: API persistence
concepts.body: Clients submit objects to the API server, which authenticates, authorizes, validates, and runs admission before persistence in etcd. A successful write does not mean containers are running. Resource versions support concurrency checks; controllers observe changes through watches and recover by listing again.

concepts.name: Scheduling
concepts.body: The scheduler considers unscheduled Pods, filters nodes using requests and placement constraints, then scores feasible nodes and binds a Pod. It does not start containers. Insufficient requested capacity leaves a Pod Pending even when measured utilization appears low.

concepts.name: Node execution
concepts.body: The kubelet observes Pods assigned to its node and coordinates image retrieval, container runtime execution, networking, and mounted storage. Image credentials or volume attachment failures happen after scheduling and require different evidence from a FailedScheduling event.

concepts.name: Convergent controllers
concepts.body: Controllers repeatedly compare desired and observed state rather than execute a manifest once. Deployment and ReplicaSet controllers create dependent objects. Their retries tolerate temporary failures, but cannot repair impossible constraints or missing permissions without an intentional configuration change.

e2e: A client submits a Deployment; admission accepts its desired replica count.
The Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet, which creates missing Pods.
The scheduler binds feasible Pods; unplaceable Pods remain Pending with events.
Kubelets start assigned containers and report status; controllers continue reconciling after failures.

tasks.name: Trace ownership
tasks.goal: Assign responsibilities without needing a live cluster.
steps: Draw API server, Deployment controller, scheduler, and kubelet. Route a three-replica request between them. Mark persistence before scheduling and container startup after binding; do not draw the scheduler writing application data.

tasks.name: Calculate feasibility
tasks.goal: Explain a Pending Pod with an offline calculation.
steps: Two nodes each have 2000m allocatable CPU and existing requests of 1500m and 1200m. A Pod requests 900m. Free requested capacity is 500m and 800m: neither fits, although their total is 1300m. Reducing replicas cannot make that individual Pod fit.

tasks.name: Classify failures
tasks.goal: Choose evidence at the correct stage.
steps: Compare FailedScheduling, ImagePullBackOff, and a rejected admission request. Assign them to scheduler, node image retrieval, and API admission respectively. For each, name one useful event or error and explain why restarting an unrelated controller would not fix it.

tasks.name: Model recovery
steps: Change the second node's existing requests to 1000m on paper. The 900m Pod now fits with 100m remaining. Explain binding, startup, and readiness separately, and identify the risk of lowering requests below the workload's real demand.

key_terms: Admission: checks before API persistence.
Binding: assigning a Pod to a node.
Reconciliation: repeated convergence toward desired state.
Allocatable: resources available for Pods after node reservations.
lesson.safety: Use fictional objects and capacity; do not edit control-plane components or shared cluster scheduling.
cleanup: Discard the paper model; no cluster resources were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a Deployment was accepted but every Pod remains Pending. How would you distinguish scheduling from startup failure?
interview_points: Check Pod scheduling conditions and events before node logs.
Compare per-node allocatable resources with requests and constraints.
Separate successful binding from image, volume, and readiness failures.

storyboard.title: From desired replicas to running containers

scenes.title: Observe demand
scenes.caption: Admission is not execution.
scenes.narration: The API holds a valid Pod that still needs a node assignment.

scenes.title: No feasible node
scenes.caption: Per-node requests exceed capacity.
scenes.narration: The scheduler cannot bind the Pod because no individual node satisfies its request.

scenes.title: Capacity becomes feasible
scenes.caption: Binding enables node startup.
scenes.narration: After capacity changes, the scheduler assigns the Pod and the kubelet can start its containers.

kubernetes/kubernetes-control-plane-sche.core: API acceptance, scheduling, container startup, and readiness are separate milestones. Use conditions and events to identify the stalled handoff; fix impossible requests rather than restarting controllers.

lesson.title: Kubernetes Pods, ReplicaSets and Deployments
lesson.why: Almost every stateless workload on Kubernetes runs as a Deployment. When a rollout stalls, a pod keeps restarting or a rollback is needed at 2 a.m., you need to know which controller owns what and what the rolling-update numbers actually mean. That is exactly what interviews test with 'walk me through a bad rollout'.
lesson.what: A **Pod** is the smallest deployable unit: one or more containers that share a network identity and volumes. A **ReplicaSet** keeps a stable number of matching Pods running. A **Deployment** manages ReplicaSets to roll out new versions at a controlled rate and keeps old ReplicaSets for rollback. You normally create Deployments and never manage their ReplicaSets directly.

concepts.name: Pods are disposable
concepts.body: Containers in a Pod share one IP and port space and can share volumes. Pods are not repaired in place: a bare Pod whose node fails is simply gone. Controllers create replacement Pods with new names and IPs, which is why clients reach workloads through a Service, not a Pod IP. Inspect ownership with `kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].kind}'`.

concepts.name: ReplicaSets keep the count; labels decide membership
concepts.body: A ReplicaSet compares the Pods matching its label selector with `replicas` and creates or deletes Pods to close the gap. Membership is by labels, so selectors must match the Pod template labels. A Deployment adds a `pod-template-hash` label so each of its ReplicaSets selects only its own Pods; the ReplicaSet is named `<deployment>-<hash>`. The Kubernetes docs say not to manage ReplicaSets owned by a Deployment.

concepts.name: Rolling updates: maxSurge and maxUnavailable
concepts.body: A rollout starts only when the Pod template (`.spec.template`) changes; scaling does not create one. With the default RollingUpdate strategy, `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable` both default to 25%. Surge rounds up and unavailable rounds down, so with 3 replicas you get at most 1 extra Pod and 0 unavailable. The new ReplicaSet scales up only as fast as new Pods become ready. `Recreate` stops all old Pods first, which causes downtime.

concepts.name: Stalled rollouts and rollback
concepts.body: If new Pods never become ready (bad image, failing readiness probe, quota), the rollout stalls while old Pods keep serving within `maxUnavailable`. After `progressDeadlineSeconds` (default 600) the Deployment reports `ProgressDeadlineExceeded`, but it does **not** roll back on its own. You run `kubectl rollout undo`. Old ReplicaSets are kept up to `revisionHistoryLimit` (default 10). The selector is immutable after creation.

e2e: `kubectl apply` sends the Deployment to the API server, which stores it.
The Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet named `<deployment>-<pod-template-hash>`.
The ReplicaSet controller creates Pods from the template until the count matches `replicas`.
The scheduler assigns each Pod to a node; the kubelet pulls the image and starts containers.
A Pod counts as available once ready for `minReadySeconds` (default 0).
Changing the image creates a new ReplicaSet; it scales up within maxSurge while the old one scales down within maxUnavailable.
If new Pods never become ready, the rollout stalls and eventually reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded.
`kubectl rollout undo` scales the previous ReplicaSet back up; old ReplicaSets beyond revisionHistoryLimit are garbage-collected.

tasks.name: Watch a ReplicaSet heal a Deployment
tasks.goal: See ownership and self-healing with your own eyes.
steps: Create a free local cluster: `kind create cluster --name lesson` (needs Docker), or open the free Killercoda Kubernetes playground in a browser.
`kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=3`
`kubectl get deploy,rs,pods --show-labels` and note the `pod-template-hash` label.
Delete one Pod with `kubectl delete pod <name>`, then run `kubectl get pods -w` and watch a replacement with a new name appear.
Print the deleted Pod's replacement owner: `kubectl get pod <new-name> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].kind}'`

tasks.name: Roll out and roll back
tasks.goal: Connect a template change to a new ReplicaSet and back again.
steps: `kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:1.28` (the container is named after the image).
`kubectl rollout status deployment/web`, then `kubectl get rs` to see two ReplicaSets.
`kubectl scale deployment/web --replicas=4` and confirm with `kubectl rollout history deployment/web` that scaling added no revision.
`kubectl rollout undo deployment/web` and check which ReplicaSet now has the Pods.

tasks.name: Diagnose a stalled rollout
tasks.goal: Prove that a bad rollout keeps old Pods serving and does not self-revert.
steps: `kubectl scale deployment/web --replicas=3`, then `kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:0.0-does-not-exist`
`kubectl rollout status deployment/web --timeout=60s` fails; `kubectl get pods` shows one new Pod in ErrImagePull or ImagePullBackOff.
Explain the numbers: with 3 replicas and 25% defaults, surge rounds up to 1 and unavailable rounds down to 0, so all 3 old Pods keep serving.
Read the reason with `kubectl describe pod <new-pod>`, then recover with `kubectl rollout undo deployment/web`.

tasks.name: Write the Deployment declaratively
tasks.goal: Own the manifest fields that control safety.
steps:
Save and `kubectl apply -f web.yaml`:
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-declarative
spec:
  replicas: 3
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-declarative
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-declarative
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.28
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
            periodSeconds: 5
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 50m
              memory: 64Mi
```
Explain why `selector.matchLabels` must match the template labels, and what happens if you later try to change the selector.
Explain what `maxUnavailable: 0` with a readiness probe guarantees during an update, and what it costs.

key_terms: Pod — one or more containers sharing a network identity and volumes; replaced, never repaired.
ReplicaSet — keeps a stable number of Pods matching its selector.
Deployment — manages ReplicaSets for controlled rollouts and rollback.
pod-template-hash — label a Deployment adds so each ReplicaSet selects only its own Pods.
maxSurge / maxUnavailable — rolling-update limits; both default to 25% (surge rounds up, unavailable down).
progressDeadlineSeconds — time before a stuck rollout reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded (default 600).
revisionHistoryLimit — how many old ReplicaSets are kept for rollback (default 10).
lesson.safety: Everything runs on a free local kind cluster (Docker required) or the free Killercoda browser playground; no cloud account is needed. The same objects work on managed clusters such as EKS, but those clusters and any LoadBalancer Services are billed.
cleanup: `kind delete cluster --name lesson` removes the whole local cluster.
On Killercoda, simply end the session.
lesson.interview_question: You deploy a new image and `kubectl rollout status` hangs. Users report no errors yet. Explain what Kubernetes is doing with the old and new Pods at this moment, how you find the cause, and exactly how you get back to a good state.
interview_points: Two ReplicaSets exist; the new one is limited by maxSurge, the old keeps serving within maxUnavailable.
Readiness gates progress: unready new Pods stall the rollout instead of taking traffic.
Diagnose with rollout status, get rs, describe pod and events (image pull, probe, quota).
The Deployment does not roll back on its own; ProgressDeadlineExceeded only reports it.
Recover with `kubectl rollout undo`, then fix and re-roll; consider maxUnavailable 0 for critical apps.
lesson.reviewed_at: 2026-09-28 (checked against the official docs listed below)

kubernetes/kubernetes-pods-deployments-a.core:
**Core idea:** you declare a Deployment; controllers do the rest.
- **Pod**: containers sharing one IP and volumes. Disposable: replaced with a new name and IP, never repaired.
- **ReplicaSet**: keeps `replicas` Pods matching its label selector. A Deployment labels each ReplicaSet's Pods with `pod-template-hash`. Don't manage those ReplicaSets yourself.
- **Deployment**: a rollout starts only when `.spec.template` changes. Scaling is not a new revision.
- **Rolling update math**: `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable` default to 25%. Surge rounds up, unavailable rounds down: 3 replicas means at most 1 extra Pod and 0 unavailable.
- **Bad rollout**: new Pods never get ready, so old Pods keep serving. After `progressDeadlineSeconds` (600 s) it reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded but does not roll back. You run `kubectl rollout undo`.

Today's exercises use a free local **kind** cluster or Killercoda, not a billed cloud cluster.

storyboard.title: Deployment rollout: two ReplicaSets and a rollback
storyboard.objective: You change the Pod template; the API server stores the new spec.

scenes.title: Desired state is stored
scenes.caption: You change the Pod template; the API server stores the new spec.
scenes.narration: Applying a new image changes the Pod template. The API server stores the Deployment. Controllers watch for that change and act on it; kubectl never starts containers itself.

scenes.title: A new ReplicaSet surges
scenes.caption: The Deployment creates ReplicaSet v2 and scales it within maxSurge.
scenes.narration: The Deployment controller creates a second ReplicaSet for the new template. With three replicas and the default limits, it adds at most one extra Pod while the old Pods keep serving.

scenes.title: Readiness gates progress
scenes.caption: Old Pods scale down only as new Pods become ready.
scenes.narration: Each new Pod must pass its readiness check before the old ReplicaSet shrinks. If new Pods never become ready, the rollout stalls and the old version keeps handling traffic.

scenes.title: Undo restores the old ReplicaSet
scenes.caption: The Deployment reports the stall; you run kubectl rollout undo.
scenes.narration: After the progress deadline, the Deployment reports that the rollout has stalled but does not revert. Rollout undo scales the previous ReplicaSet back up from the saved revision history.

lesson.title: Kubernetes readiness liveness and startup probes
lesson.why: The wrong health check can turn a dependency outage into a restart storm. Each probe should answer a different operational question.
lesson.what: Design startup, readiness, and liveness checks around application lifecycle rather than reusing one expensive endpoint everywhere.

concepts.name: Startup protection
concepts.body: A configured startup probe suppresses liveness and readiness checks until it succeeds. It accommodates measured initialization work without permanently weakening failure detection. Exceeding its failure threshold causes container restart; a large budget still cannot repair a permanently broken initialization dependency.

concepts.name: Readiness eligibility
concepts.body: Readiness controls whether a Pod is considered ready for ordinary Service traffic. Failure does not restart the container. Endpoint propagation and in-flight connections are not instantaneous, so an application still needs graceful shutdown and appropriate connection draining during termination.

concepts.name: Liveness recovery
concepts.body: Liveness detects conditions a container restart can plausibly repair, such as an internal deadlock. Checking every remote dependency here is dangerous: a database outage could restart every otherwise healthy replica, increase connection pressure, and prolong recovery instead of restoring service.

concepts.name: Signals and budgets
concepts.body: HTTP, TCP, exec, and supported gRPC probes offer different evidence. TCP only proves that a port accepts connections. Tune period, timeout, and failure thresholds from measured behavior, balancing detection delay against false failures during transient CPU or IO pressure.

e2e: A container starts while its startup probe protects initialization work.
Startup succeeds, enabling independent readiness and liveness evaluations.
Readiness failure removes ordinary traffic eligibility without restarting the process.
An internal unrecoverable hang fails liveness; the kubelet restarts and rechecks startup.

tasks.name: Separate health contracts
tasks.goal: Define three endpoints with different meanings.
steps: For a catalog service, describe /startup as cache initialization complete, /ready as able to serve supported requests, and /live as event loop responsive. Explain whether a recommendations dependency should block all traffic when recommendations can be omitted.

tasks.name: Calculate startup allowance
tasks.goal: Compute an offline probe timing budget.
steps: Use periodSeconds=5 and failureThreshold=24 with initialDelaySeconds=0. Their product gives a nominal 120-second startup allowance, not an exact wall-clock guarantee. A measured 75-second startup fits; a permanent 503 still eventually triggers restart. Account separately for probe duration and scheduling.

tasks.name: Diagnose a restart loop
tasks.goal: Connect remote failures with excessive restarts.
steps: Assume /live returns 503 whenever the database is unavailable. Trace database failure to liveness failures, restarts, and new connection bursts. Redesign liveness around internal responsiveness and decide whether readiness should fail or the service should offer reduced functionality.

tasks.name: Test termination behavior
steps: Write a timeline of readiness loss, endpoint propagation, connection draining, and process exit. Allow in-flight requests a bounded grace period. Describe why a passing readiness probe immediately before termination cannot guarantee that every subsequent request reaches a live process.

key_terms: Readiness: eligibility to serve traffic.
Liveness: restart-worthy process health.
Startup probe: initialization gate for other probes.
Failure threshold: consecutive failures required for action.
lesson.safety: Use endpoint descriptions and timing calculations only; never intentionally fail shared production health checks.
cleanup: Discard the fictional timing table; no processes or workloads were started.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a database outage causes every application Pod to restart repeatedly. How would you redesign its probes?
interview_points: Separate dependency readiness from process liveness.
Provide bounded startup allowance based on measured initialization.
Validate reduced functionality and graceful connection draining.

storyboard.title: Three probes, three different decisions
storyboard.objective: Prevent dependency outages from causing restart storms.

scenes.title: Initialize safely
scenes.caption: Startup gates the other checks.
scenes.narration: The kubelet allows bounded initialization before evaluating ordinary readiness and liveness.

scenes.title: Lose readiness
scenes.caption: Traffic eligibility is not process life.
scenes.narration: The application cannot serve requests, so readiness fails without requiring a container restart.

scenes.title: Serve again
scenes.caption: Recovery does not require restarting healthy code.
scenes.narration: After the dependency recovers, readiness passes and endpoint updates restore traffic eligibility.

kubernetes/kubernetes-readiness-liveness.core: Startup protects initialization, readiness gates traffic, and liveness decides restart. Dependency failures rarely belong in liveness; account for endpoint propagation and graceful shutdown.
prerequisites: Container lifecycle and HTTP status codes

lesson.title: Kubernetes services endpoints ingress and Gateway API
lesson.why: A healthy Pod does not prove that a client can reach it. Service discovery and external routing add independent selectors, ports, and controller behavior.
lesson.what: Trace traffic through a Service and its EndpointSlices, then distinguish Ingress configuration from Gateway API infrastructure and routes.

concepts.name: Stable Service identity
concepts.body: A ClusterIP Service exposes a stable virtual address and DNS name while backend Pod addresses change. Its selector identifies matching Pods, and targetPort identifies the receiving application port. A Service is not itself an application process listening inside a Pod.

concepts.name: EndpointSlice membership
concepts.body: EndpointSlices describe backend addresses, ports, and readiness-related conditions. A label mismatch can leave a valid Service with no backends. Inspect selectors, readiness, and target ports separately; changing external DNS cannot repair empty backend membership inside the cluster.

concepts.name: Ingress responsibilities
concepts.body: An Ingress declares HTTP routing, commonly by host and path, but requires a compatible controller to implement it. A resource without a controller may do nothing. TLS termination, annotations, and supported capabilities depend on the implementation rather than the YAML kind alone.

concepts.name: Gateway separation
concepts.body: Gateway API separates infrastructure ownership through GatewayClass and Gateway from application routes such as HTTPRoute. Listener attachment, namespace permissions, and reference rules govern connectivity. Accepted configuration and resolved backend references are important status signals; not every controller supports every optional feature.

e2e: The controller accepts an external listener and a route matching host and path.
The route selects a Service backend and an exposed Service port.
The Service implementation forwards toward eligible addresses listed by EndpointSlices.
The application receives traffic on targetPort; failures are localized along these separate handoffs.

tasks.name: Map port translation
steps: Draw client HTTPS 443 to a TLS-terminating gateway, Service port 80, and targetPort 8080. Label the encryption boundary. Explain why changing containerPort metadata alone does not make an application begin listening on 8080.

tasks.name: Compute backend membership
tasks.goal: Work a complete selector example offline.
steps: A Service selects app=shop. Pod A has app=shop and ready=true; B has app=shop and ready=false; C has app=other and ready=true. Under ordinary ready-only routing, A is the sole eligible backend. Making B ready adds B; changing C's port does not match its label.

tasks.name: Diagnose an empty route
tasks.goal: Order checks from configuration to application.
steps: A route exists but returns backend-unavailable errors. Check route acceptance and resolved references, Service name and port, EndpointSlice addresses, then application listening behavior. Explain why a route can be accepted even while no healthy endpoint serves requests.

tasks.name: Design team boundaries
steps: Give a platform team ownership of GatewayClass and listeners, and an application team ownership of its HTTPRoute. Specify permitted namespaces and backend reference approval. Compare that separation with controller-specific Ingress annotations, including portability and operational complexity trade-offs.

key_terms: ClusterIP: stable internal Service address.
EndpointSlice: grouped backend addresses and conditions.
Ingress: declarative HTTP routing resource.
HTTPRoute: Gateway API HTTP routing configuration.
lesson.safety: Use paper routes and fictional hostnames; do not expose a local or shared service publicly.
cleanup: Remove the offline routing diagram only; no DNS or load balancers were changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, your gateway accepts an HTTPRoute but requests fail despite a running Pod. Which layers would you inspect?
interview_points: Check route conditions, backend references, and Service ports.
Verify label selection and ready EndpointSlice membership.
Test application listening and network policy after configuration checks.

storyboard.title: A route needs a healthy Service backend
storyboard.objective: Separate routing acceptance from backend reachability.

scenes.title: Route accepted
scenes.caption: The listener forwards to a Service.
scenes.narration: A matching request reaches the Service selected by the accepted HTTPRoute.

scenes.title: No ready endpoint
scenes.caption: A valid Service can have no usable backend.
scenes.narration: The selected Pod is not ready, leaving the Service without an eligible destination.

scenes.title: Backend recovers
scenes.caption: Readiness completes the traffic path.
scenes.narration: The Pod becomes ready and endpoint information allows forwarding to the application port.

kubernetes/kubernetes-services-endpoints.core: Trace listener, route, Service port, EndpointSlice, and application targetPort separately. Ingress and Gateway objects require implementing controllers; accepted routes do not guarantee ready backends.

lesson.title: Kubernetes CNI network policies and DNS
lesson.why: Network isolation often fails through assumptions about implementation or DNS. A policy object cannot enforce rules unless the installed network implementation supports them.
lesson.what: Connect Pod networking, additive NetworkPolicy rules, and cluster DNS while designing a minimal service-to-service communication matrix.

concepts.name: CNI implementation
concepts.body: The container network interface integrates runtime networking with plugins that assign connectivity and addresses. Kubernetes defines a networking model but does not provide every implementation itself. Routing, encapsulation, policy enforcement, and observability vary, so verify actual plugin capabilities before relying on a policy.

concepts.name: Isolation selection
concepts.body: A NetworkPolicy selects Pods within its namespace. Selecting ingress or egress isolation changes that direction from unrestricted to permitted-by-policy. Allowed traffic is additive across applicable policies; one deny-looking policy cannot override another policy that permits the same connection.

concepts.name: Two-sided authorization
concepts.body: When both ends are isolated, source egress and destination ingress must permit a connection. Namespace selectors match namespace labels, not arbitrary namespace names. Combining namespaceSelector and podSelector in one peer narrows matching; separate peers provide alternative matches and therefore broaden access.

concepts.name: DNS dependency
concepts.body: Applications resolving service names need access to their actual DNS path, commonly cluster DNS or a node-local cache. Permit relevant UDP and TCP DNS traffic according to the implementation. Successful name resolution does not establish application-port access, and direct-IP success does not prove DNS works.

e2e: The network plugin gives a new Pod connectivity consistent with the cluster model.
Policies selecting that Pod isolate the specified ingress or egress direction.
A name lookup requires a separately allowed path to the configured resolver.
The application connection succeeds only when routing and both applicable policy directions allow it.

tasks.name: Build a traffic matrix
tasks.goal: State intended access before writing rules.
steps: List frontend to API on TCP 8080, API to database on TCP 5432, and both workloads to the resolver. Explicitly exclude frontend to database. Include namespace labels and explain which component must enforce each boundary.

tasks.name: Evaluate additive rules
tasks.goal: Calculate the allowed connection set offline.
steps: Policy A permits source egress ports {53,8080}; policy B permits {443}. Their union is {53,443,8080}. If destination ingress allows only 8080, the modeled application connection on 8080 passes both sides while 443 fails destination ingress. DNS still needs its own resolver destination and protocols.

tasks.name: Diagnose DNS isolation
tasks.goal: Distinguish resolution failure from application denial.
steps: Assume connecting to an allowed API address succeeds while resolving its Service name times out after egress isolation. Inspect resolver configuration and DNS allowances first. Explain why permitting arbitrary internet egress is a broader and weaker fix than a specific resolver path.

tasks.name: Review selector scope
steps: Compare a single peer containing namespace and Pod selectors with two separate peers. Work through a Pod matching only the namespace selector: the combined peer excludes it, while the alternative peer permits it. Record the narrower intended structure in your diagram.

key_terms: CNI: runtime network plugin interface.
Isolation: restricting a selected traffic direction.
Peer: allowed connection source or destination selector.
DNS: mapping names to address records.
lesson.safety: Do not apply deny-all rules to shared namespaces; use an offline matrix with synthetic addresses.
cleanup: Discard the matrix after review; no network rules require removal.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, an egress policy breaks Service names but direct-address calls still work. How do you restore only necessary connectivity?
interview_points: Inspect the workload's actual DNS resolver path.
Permit narrowly scoped UDP and TCP DNS as needed.
Verify plugin enforcement and application ingress independently.

storyboard.title: DNS is a separate network dependency
storyboard.objective: Show why application-port allowance is insufficient.

scenes.title: Resolve and call
scenes.caption: Two paths serve one application request.
scenes.narration: The application resolves the Service name and connects to the API on its allowed port.

scenes.title: DNS blocked
scenes.caption: Port 8080 allowance cannot resolve names.
scenes.narration: Egress isolation omits the resolver path, so requests by name fail before contacting the API.

scenes.title: Narrow resolver allowance
scenes.caption: Restore DNS without opening all egress.
scenes.narration: A resolver-specific allowance restores name lookup while application and database boundaries remain constrained.

kubernetes/kubernetes-cni-network-polici.core: NetworkPolicies are additive and require an enforcing implementation. Both isolated directions must allow traffic. DNS needs an explicit path; combined peer selectors narrow scope while separate peers broaden it.

lesson.title: Kubernetes persistent volumes CSI and StatefulSets
lesson.why: Replacing a Pod is easy; preserving the right data through replacement requires explicit identity, storage lifecycle, and recovery decisions.
lesson.what: Follow a claim from provisioning to attachment and connect StatefulSet identity with storage behavior without treating replication as backup.

concepts.name: Claims and volumes
concepts.body: A PersistentVolumeClaim requests capacity and access characteristics. It binds to a PersistentVolume, either precreated or provisioned through a StorageClass. Binding is a control-plane decision; mounting the resulting volume on a node is a later step that can fail independently.

concepts.name: CSI lifecycle
concepts.body: CSI drivers integrate provisioning, attachment, mounting, and supported snapshot or expansion operations. Capabilities differ by driver. WaitForFirstConsumer can defer binding until scheduling constraints are known, avoiding a volume selected in a topology where the workload cannot run.

concepts.name: Stateful identity
concepts.body: StatefulSets provide stable ordinal identities and support per-Pod claims through volumeClaimTemplates. A restarted or replaced ordinal can reconnect to its own data. Stable identity is not database replication: the application must still implement consistency, failover, and protection against concurrent unsafe writers.

concepts.name: Retention and recovery
concepts.body: Reclaim policy governs what happens to storage after claim release, while StatefulSet claim retention is a separate configuration. ReadWriteOnce generally limits read-write mounting to one node, not necessarily one Pod. Backups need application-consistent capture and tested restore, not simply healthy mounted volumes.

e2e: A StatefulSet requests an ordinal-specific claim with a StorageClass and capacity.
The provisioner creates suitable storage after any topology-aware scheduling decision.
The driver attaches and mounts storage before the container can use its files.
A replacement Pod reuses intended identity and data; operators verify application recovery and backup coverage.

tasks.name: Trace a claim
steps: Draw StatefulSet ledger, Pod ledger-0, claim data-ledger-0, and its bound volume. Mark which identity survives a Pod replacement. Explain why a bound claim does not prove that the node can mount the filesystem successfully.

tasks.name: Calculate storage footprint
tasks.goal: Work an exact provisioning estimate offline.
steps: Three replicas each request a 12 GiB claim, giving 36 GiB logical requested storage. Keeping two complete uncompressed backup copies adds 72 GiB, for 108 GiB before provider overhead. Reducing replicas to two does not automatically imply deletion of the third claim; inspect retention policy.

tasks.name: Diagnose topology mismatch
steps: Assume a prebound volume belongs to zone A while node affinity requires zone B. Explain why extra CPU in B cannot help. Compare topology-compatible placement with deferred binding, and distinguish this conflict from a CSI attachment permission failure.

tasks.name: Plan a restore drill
tasks.goal: Prove data recovery rather than Pod recovery.
steps: Define a synthetic ledger containing three numbered records. Describe restoring a backup into an isolated claim, verifying all records and database integrity, and measuring elapsed recovery time. Preserve the source claim until verification; never test by deleting the only data copy.

key_terms: PVC: namespaced request for persistent storage.
PV: cluster storage resource bound to a claim.
CSI: storage driver integration interface.
Reclaim policy: storage disposition after claim release.
lesson.safety: Use fictional claims; storage deletion and reclaim-policy changes can permanently destroy real data.
cleanup: Discard calculations only; no volumes, claims, snapshots, or cloud disks were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a StatefulSet Pod is Pending despite a bound claim and idle nodes. How would you investigate without risking its data?
interview_points: Check scheduling topology and volume node affinity.
Separate binding, attachment, mounting, and application recovery.
Preserve source data and inspect reclaim and retention behavior.

storyboard.title: Stable identity depends on compatible storage
storyboard.objective: Trace provisioning, topology failure, and safe reuse.

scenes.title: Request ordinal storage
scenes.caption: Each replica gets its intended claim.
scenes.narration: The StatefulSet gives an ordinal its own storage request rather than an interchangeable empty filesystem.

scenes.title: Topology blocks progress
scenes.caption: Binding and placement must agree.
scenes.narration: A volume in another zone cannot satisfy the Pod's placement constraints, even when CPU is available.

scenes.title: Use compatible placement
scenes.caption: Mount before application recovery.
scenes.narration: Compatible scheduling and driver operations allow the replacement ordinal to mount its preserved data.

kubernetes/kubernetes-persistent-volumes.core: PVC binding, CSI attachment, and application recovery are separate. StatefulSet identity does not supply replication or backups. Check topology, reclaim policy, claim retention, and tested restore paths.
objectives: Plan StatefulSet data retention and recovery

lesson.title: Kubernetes ConfigMaps Secrets and workload configuration
lesson.why: Configuration changes can create inconsistent replicas or expose credentials even when application code has not changed. Delivery and reload semantics must be explicit.
lesson.what: Choose environment variables or projected files deliberately, distinguish encoding from confidentiality, and design observable configuration rollout.

concepts.name: Configuration separation
concepts.body: ConfigMaps store nonconfidential configuration; Secrets represent sensitive data but their familiar base64 representation is only encoding. Protect Secret API access, storage encryption, and node access. A user allowed to create workloads may indirectly read secrets mounted by those workloads.

concepts.name: Environment snapshots
concepts.body: Environment variables sourced from ConfigMaps or Secrets are resolved when containers start. Updating the source does not modify a running process environment. A controlled rollout is needed, and the application should expose a nonsecret configuration version to diagnose mixed populations.

concepts.name: Projected files
concepts.body: Mounted configuration can update eventually through kubelet synchronization, but the application must reload it correctly. A subPath mount does not receive ordinary projected updates. Atomic replacement patterns also mean applications should reopen files rather than assume a held file descriptor sees new bytes.

concepts.name: Versioned rollout
concepts.body: Immutable or versioned configuration objects make rollout intent explicit and support reproducible rollback. They increase object lifecycle management, so remove old objects only after confirming no workload references them. Secret rotation may require an overlap period where old and new credentials both work.

e2e: An operator creates validated configuration separately from the application image.
A Pod references the selected version through environment variables or mounted files.
A change reaches new containers or updated projections according to the chosen delivery mechanism.
The application reloads or rolls out, reports a safe version marker, and retires unused configuration.

tasks.name: Choose delivery mechanisms
steps: Classify a startup-only feature mode, a dynamically reloaded routing table, and a database password. Select environment or file delivery for each, document reload behavior, and keep the password out of ConfigMaps, logs, and examples.

tasks.name: Decode without secrecy claims
tasks.goal: Verify an exact safe local operation.
steps: Run python -c "import base64; print(base64.b64decode('ZGVtby1vbmx5').decode())". Expected output is demo-only. This synthetic value proves that base64 is reversible encoding, not encryption; do not substitute a real token or paste credentials into shell history.

tasks.name: Diagnose mixed replicas
tasks.goal: Explain inconsistent configuration after an update.
steps: Three replicas source MODE from environment variables. Update the ConfigMap on paper and restart only one replica. Predict one new value and two old values. Design a template-version change and readiness check so the rollout becomes visible and bounded.

tasks.name: Design safe rotation
steps: Write a sequence that issues a new synthetic credential, enables overlapping validity, updates the Secret, reloads all clients, verifies success, then revokes the old credential. State what must be checked before deleting the old Secret version and how failed clients are identified without logging credentials.

key_terms: ConfigMap: nonsecret configuration object.
Secret: access-controlled sensitive configuration object.
Projection: exposing object data as mounted files.
Rotation: replacing credentials with a controlled validity transition.
lesson.safety: Use only the supplied demo string; never print, decode, or commit real credentials during practice.
cleanup: No persistent files are needed; remove any personal scratch notes containing only synthetic values.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, half your replicas use old configuration after a ConfigMap update. What determines whether reload or rollout is needed?
interview_points: Identify environment, projected-volume, or subPath delivery.
Check application reload semantics and safe version markers.
Plan bounded rollout and credential overlap where required.

storyboard.title: Updating configuration is not updating every process
storyboard.objective: Explain source updates versus application reload.

scenes.title: Read at startup
scenes.caption: Environment values are snapshots.
scenes.narration: The existing container receives its environment when it starts, not continuously afterward.

scenes.title: Source changes
scenes.caption: Old processes retain their environment.
scenes.narration: Updating the configuration object leaves the running container on the prior value.

scenes.title: Controlled replacement
scenes.caption: A new container reads the new version.
scenes.narration: A bounded rollout starts replacements and verifies a nonsecret version marker before retiring old replicas.

kubernetes/kubernetes-configmaps-secrets.core: ConfigMap and Secret updates have delivery-specific effects: environment requires restart, projected files require reload, and subPath does not receive ordinary updates. Base64 is not encryption.

lesson.title: Kubernetes RBAC service accounts and workload identity
lesson.why: A workload identity is useful only when its permissions and trust boundaries are narrow. Cluster authorization and cloud authorization are different decisions.
lesson.what: Model Kubernetes service accounts, role bindings, short-lived tokens, and external federation without issuing real credentials.

concepts.name: Namespaced workload identity
concepts.body: A ServiceAccount supplies an identity for workloads in one namespace. Projected tokens can have bounded audiences and lifetimes. Disable automatic mounting when the application does not need API access, and do not treat a token copied from one environment as a reusable deployment credential.

concepts.name: RBAC evaluation
concepts.body: Roles and ClusterRoles describe allowed verbs on resources, sometimes narrowed by resource names. RoleBindings grant permissions within a namespace, even when referring to a ClusterRole; ClusterRoleBindings grant cluster-wide scope. Kubernetes RBAC is additive and has no explicit deny rule.

concepts.name: Privilege paths
concepts.body: Reading Secrets, creating privileged workloads, impersonating identities, or changing role bindings can produce broader access than a simple resource count suggests. Least privilege reviews therefore examine reachable capabilities, not just role names. Wildcard permissions also include future resources or verbs and deserve special scrutiny.

concepts.name: External federation
concepts.body: Workload identity federation exchanges a trusted Kubernetes identity token for an external provider credential under configured trust conditions. The external provider validates issuer, audience, and subject, then applies its own permissions. Kubernetes RBAC alone neither authorizes cloud storage access nor constrains that provider's role.

e2e: A Pod starts with a selected ServiceAccount and only required token projection.
The API authenticates its token and evaluates applicable RBAC grants for a request.
A separate federation service may validate that identity for an external credential exchange.
The external service evaluates its own policy; audit records must connect both authorization boundaries.

tasks.name: Draw identity boundaries
steps: Sketch a reports Pod, ServiceAccount reports-reader, Kubernetes API, and fictional object store. Mark the Kubernetes role binding on one path and external trust plus storage permission on the other. Explain why a cluster-admin role is unnecessary for reading one external object prefix.

tasks.name: Evaluate effective rights
steps: Role A permits get and list on ConfigMaps in team-a; Role B permits watch there. Their combined verbs are get, list, watch. A delete request is denied without another grant. A RoleBinding in team-a does not grant the same rights in team-b, even when it references a ClusterRole.

tasks.name: Diagnose denied federation
steps: Assume a Pod can list allowed ConfigMaps but external token exchange fails. Check issuer, audience, subject, and trust configuration before expanding Kubernetes permissions. Contrast an exchange rejection with a successful exchange followed by object-store AccessDenied.

tasks.name: Review excess capability
steps: A proposed role adds create Pods and get Secrets to a metrics reader. Explain how mounting a more privileged identity or reading credentials broadens access. Replace those grants with the exact metrics access needed, and specify a periodic access review using synthetic identities.

key_terms: ServiceAccount: namespaced workload identity.
RoleBinding: namespace-scoped permission assignment.
Audience: intended token recipient.
Federation: exchanging trusted identity across authorization systems.
lesson.safety: Do not retrieve live tokens, bind privileged roles, or test access against real external accounts.
cleanup: Discard the synthetic permission matrix; no tokens or role bindings were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a Pod can access the Kubernetes API but cannot read cloud storage. How would you troubleshoot without granting administrator access?
interview_points: Distinguish token exchange failure from external resource denial.
Verify issuer, audience, subject, and narrow external permissions.
Avoid unrelated Kubernetes role expansion and long-lived tokens.

storyboard.title: Two authorization systems, one workload
storyboard.objective: Separate cluster RBAC from external federation.

scenes.title: Cluster access succeeds
scenes.caption: A RoleBinding authorizes a narrow request.
scenes.narration: The workload reads permitted configuration through Kubernetes RBAC.

scenes.title: External trust rejects
scenes.caption: Cluster access does not imply cloud access.
scenes.narration: The external provider rejects a token with the wrong audience despite valid cluster permissions.

scenes.title: Correct the trust boundary
scenes.caption: Fix audience and subject, not cluster privilege.
scenes.narration: A correctly scoped token exchange supplies an external identity whose own permissions still limit storage access.

kubernetes/kubernetes-rbac-service-accou.core: ServiceAccounts identify workloads; RBAC authorizes cluster requests additively. External federation validates issuer, subject, and audience before separate provider policies apply. Diagnose the failed boundary.
objectives: Separate federation trust from resource authorization

lesson.title: Kubernetes requests limits QoS and eviction
lesson.why: Low average utilization does not rule out resource failure. Scheduling reservations, runtime enforcement, and node pressure use different signals and policies.
lesson.what: Distinguish CPU throttling, memory termination, and node eviction using a fictional workload capacity model.

concepts.name: Requests reserve placement
concepts.body: The scheduler uses requests to determine whether Pods fit on a node. Requests are not preallocated physical memory and do not cap all consumption. Setting them too low can admit more demand than the node can safely support when workloads become busy together.

concepts.name: Limits constrain runtime
concepts.body: CPU limits typically throttle execution when a container exhausts its quota. Memory limits are enforced reactively and may produce an OOM termination. More CPU can improve latency only when CPU is the bottleneck; increasing memory limits cannot repair a sustained leak.

concepts.name: Quality of service
concepts.body: Guaranteed, Burstable, and BestEffort classes reflect resource configuration. Under the standard per-container model, Guaranteed requires equal CPU and memory requests and limits for every container. QoS influences resource management but does not promise that a Pod can never be killed or evicted.

concepts.name: Node pressure
concepts.body: The kubelet may evict Pods to reclaim memory, disk space, or inodes. Ranking considers factors including usage relative to requests and priority, not simply a universal QoS ordering. Inspect events, termination reasons, node conditions, and application metrics before changing resource configuration.

e2e: Requests are compared with node allocatable capacity before Pod binding.
Runtime limits constrain execution after containers begin consuming resources.
A memory breach may kill a container; node pressure may instead evict a Pod.
Controllers replace missing Pods while operators correct demand, reservations, or node capacity.

tasks.name: Size a reservation
steps: A node has 4000m allocatable CPU. Existing requests total 2500m, leaving 1500m. Three new Pods requesting 600m each require 1800m, so only two fit before other constraints. Their combined limits do not replace this request-based scheduling calculation.

tasks.name: Classify symptoms
steps: Match high CPU throttling to quota, OOMKilled to memory termination evidence, and Evicted with DiskPressure to node reclamation. Explain why increasing a CPU limit cannot repair exhausted disk inodes and why checking the previous container log may reveal a memory leak.

tasks.name: Choose QoS deliberately
steps: Profile A sets every container to CPU request=limit=500m and memory request=limit=256Mi. Profile B omits all requests and limits. Under the standard model they are Guaranteed and BestEffort. Discuss utilization flexibility, measurement uncertainty, and why neither label substitutes for application redundancy.

tasks.name: Plan measured adjustment
steps: Assume a 256Mi memory limit fails only during a documented 320Mi initialization peak. Propose measuring steady usage, increasing bounded startup headroom, and checking node fit. Contrast this with steadily increasing memory over hours, where a leak fix and alert are more appropriate.

key_terms: Request: scheduling reservation.
Limit: runtime resource constraint.
Throttling: delayed CPU execution.
Eviction: kubelet removal of a Pod.
lesson.safety: Use calculations only; do not stress host memory or fill disks.
cleanup: Discard the fictional resource table; no workloads were launched.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a low-CPU service restarts during traffic bursts. How would you distinguish memory pressure from CPU throttling?
interview_points: Inspect termination reasons and node events.
Compare requests, limits, and measured peaks.
Change the demonstrated bottleneck and verify recovery.

storyboard.title: Placement and runtime use different resource signals

scenes.title: Reserve placement
scenes.caption: Requests fit.
scenes.narration: The scheduler places the Pod using its declared requests.

scenes.title: Memory exceeds limit
scenes.caption: Placement did not guarantee unlimited memory.
scenes.narration: The running container exceeds its memory limit and is terminated.

scenes.title: Correct measured demand
scenes.caption: Fix the cause before repeating.
scenes.narration: A measured memory profile informs a safe limit and reservation adjustment.

kubernetes/kubernetes-requests-limits-qo.core: Requests guide scheduling; limits constrain runtime. CPU throttling, OOM termination, and node eviction need different evidence and remedies.

lesson.title: Kubernetes HPA VPA and cluster autoscaling
lesson.why: Autoscaling is a feedback system, not instant spare capacity. Mixing incompatible controllers can create oscillation or leave demand waiting for nodes.
lesson.what: Connect horizontal replicas, vertical sizing, and node capacity while calculating a simple utilization-driven scale decision.

concepts.name: Horizontal scaling
concepts.body: The HPA adjusts replica counts from configured resource, custom, or external metrics. CPU utilization commonly means usage relative to requests, not limits or node capacity. Missing requests or missing metrics can prevent the intended calculation, and readiness handling dampens decisions for new Pods.

concepts.name: Vertical sizing
concepts.body: The VPA recommends or adjusts resource requests according to its mode and supported capabilities. Applying changes may require eviction and recreation, depending on configuration and platform support. Combining CPU-driven HPA with VPA changing CPU requests can move the HPA denominator and create conflicting feedback.

concepts.name: Node supply
concepts.body: A cluster autoscaler or other node provisioner adds capacity in response to schedulable demand, commonly Pending Pods with unsatisfied requests. It cannot overcome unsupported instance shapes, quota exhaustion, or impossible placement constraints. Node startup, image pulls, and application warmup all add delay.

concepts.name: Stability and bounds
concepts.body: Minimum and maximum replicas, scaling policies, stabilization windows, and sensible metrics limit oscillation. Queue depth can better represent asynchronous work than CPU. Scale-down must respect workload lifecycle and disruption constraints, while scheduled demand may justify prewarming rather than waiting for reactive scale-out.

e2e: A demand signal rises above the target while current replicas remain busy.
HPA calculates and bounds a desired replica count, creating additional Pods.
Unschedulable demand prompts node provisioning when supported capacity is available.
New nodes and Pods become ready; metrics settle and stabilization limits premature scale-down.

tasks.name: Compute desired replicas
tasks.goal: Apply the basic HPA formula offline.
steps: With four replicas, current utilization 75 percent, and target 50 percent, calculate ceil(4*75/50)=6 replicas. This simplified example excludes tolerance and missing metrics. If maxReplicas is five, the configured bound limits the result to five rather than guaranteeing target utilization.

tasks.name: Map control loops
steps: Draw HPA changing replica count, VPA changing requests, and node provisioning changing available capacity. Explain which component handles a single Pod requesting more memory than any allowed node shape and why simply raising HPA maxReplicas cannot make it fit.

tasks.name: Diagnose feedback conflict
steps: A Pod consumes 300m CPU with a 500m request, reporting 60 percent utilization. VPA raises the request to 1000m while usage stays constant; utilization becomes 30 percent. Describe why CPU-based HPA might now reduce replicas despite unchanged work demand.

tasks.name: Design burst protection
steps: For a sudden queue burst, choose a queue-based metric, bounded backlog, minimum warm replicas, and maximum spend guardrail. List quota, node startup, and model warmup as separate delays. Define what happens to new work when all scaling limits are reached.

key_terms: HPA: horizontal replica autoscaler.
VPA: vertical resource sizing controller.
Stabilization: damping recent scaling decisions.
Provisioner: controller supplying node capacity.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic metrics; do not run load generators or enable paid node growth.
cleanup: Discard the feedback diagram; no scaling settings changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, HPA increases replicas but latency remains high and new Pods stay Pending. What should you inspect?
interview_points: Check metric validity and replica bounds.
Inspect requests, placement, node shapes, and quota.
Measure provisioning and readiness delay separately.

storyboard.title: Replica demand still needs node supply
storyboard.objective: Trace the two coupled scaling loops.

scenes.title: Demand rises
scenes.caption: HPA requests replicas.
scenes.narration: A valid utilization signal increases the desired replica count.

scenes.title: Pods wait
scenes.caption: Replica count is not ready capacity.
scenes.narration: New Pods remain Pending because existing nodes cannot fit their requests.

scenes.title: Supply catches up
scenes.caption: Provisioning and startup take time.
scenes.narration: Compatible new nodes allow scheduling, followed by application warmup and readiness.

kubernetes/kubernetes-hpa-vpa-and-cluste.core: HPA changes replicas, VPA changes sizing, and node autoscaling changes supply. CPU requests affect HPA utilization; account for controller interaction, bounds, and warmup.

lesson.title: Kubernetes affinity taints tolerations and topology spread
lesson.why: Replica count alone does not protect against a rack or zone failure. Placement policy must express both isolation and distribution without making Pods impossible to schedule.
lesson.what: Compare node affinity, inter-Pod affinity, taints, and topology spread using a small offline scheduling matrix.

concepts.name: Node selection
concepts.body: Node affinity matches node labels using hard requirements or soft preferences. Required rules filter candidates; preferred rules affect scoring only among feasible nodes. Labels used for security-sensitive isolation need trustworthy administration rather than arbitrary mutable labels controlled by the workload owner.

concepts.name: Pod relationships
concepts.body: Pod affinity and anti-affinity place workloads relative to other labeled Pods within a topology domain. They can co-locate chatty services or separate replicas, but hard rules consume placement flexibility and can make upgrades stall when eligible domains are temporarily unavailable.

concepts.name: Taints and tolerations
concepts.body: Taints repel Pods unless matching tolerations permit them. A toleration does not attract a Pod or reserve the node exclusively. NoSchedule blocks new placement, PreferNoSchedule is softer, and NoExecute can also evict existing non-tolerating Pods according to applicable tolerance behavior.

concepts.name: Topology balance
concepts.body: Topology spread limits skew across eligible domains such as zones or hostnames. maxSkew, topology keys, and whenUnsatisfiable determine whether imbalance blocks scheduling or merely affects preference. Eligibility and minimum-domain settings matter; counting every visible node as a usable domain gives misleading availability claims.

e2e: The scheduler filters nodes using required affinity and other feasibility rules.
Taints remove candidates lacking the necessary tolerations.
Topology and Pod relationship rules constrain or score remaining placements.
If no node satisfies hard constraints, the Pod stays Pending until policy or capacity changes.

tasks.name: Compute a balanced placement
steps: Three eligible zones hold matching replica counts 2,2,1. With maxSkew=1 and ordinary minimum count one, placing the next replica in zone three produces 2,2,2. Placing it in zone one produces 3,2,1 and skew two, violating a hard spread constraint in this simplified case.

tasks.name: Separate permission from attraction
steps: A GPU node has a gpu=true:NoSchedule taint. Give a batch Pod a matching toleration and observe that it could still choose another feasible node. Add required node affinity for the GPU label on paper, then describe why both controls serve different purposes.

tasks.name: Diagnose contradictory constraints
steps: Require zone=A and disk=fast when all fast disks are in zone B. Write candidate sets for each rule and show their intersection is empty. Explain why adding replicas or relaxing a soft preference cannot resolve these contradictory hard requirements.

tasks.name: Review failure tolerance
steps: Place three replicas across three zones, then remove one eligible zone from the model. Compare strict anti-affinity with a preference and document whether two replicas or Pending replacements are acceptable. Keep the intended failure-domain guarantee explicit rather than silently relaxing every rule.

key_terms: Affinity: attraction through placement rules.
Taint: node repulsion signal.
Toleration: permission to tolerate a taint.
Skew: difference in matching counts across eligible domains.
lesson.safety: Use paper node labels; changing shared taints can evict or strand real workloads.
cleanup: Discard your placement matrix; no node metadata was changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a Pod tolerates the GPU taint but lands on a CPU node. Why, and how would you constrain it correctly?
interview_points: A toleration permits but does not select placement.
Use required affinity for trustworthy GPU node labels.
Check capacity and topology interactions before enforcing hard constraints.

storyboard.title: Scheduling is an intersection of constraints
storyboard.objective: Explain feasible placement and impossible rules.

scenes.title: Evaluate candidates
scenes.caption: Different rules select different nodes.
scenes.narration: The Pod needs both its required zone and its required disk label.

scenes.title: Empty intersection
scenes.caption: Neither group satisfies both requirements.
scenes.narration: Fast disks exist only in zone B while required affinity demands zone A.

scenes.title: Correct intentional placement
scenes.caption: Change a requirement only after review.
scenes.narration: Providing compatible capacity or correcting the zone requirement creates a feasible candidate.

kubernetes/kubernetes-affinity-taints-to.core: Hard constraints intersect; soft preferences score feasible nodes. Tolerations permit rather than attract. Spread across eligible failure domains while retaining a deliberate upgrade strategy.

lesson.title: Kubernetes disruption budgets draining and upgrades
lesson.why: Routine maintenance can cause outages when too much capacity disappears at once. Disruption budgets help coordinate voluntary evictions but cannot prevent every failure.
lesson.what: Model safe node maintenance with availability budgets, replacement capacity, graceful termination, and explicit stop conditions.

concepts.name: Budget scope
concepts.body: A PodDisruptionBudget limits eligible voluntary disruptions through the eviction API for selected Pods. It does not prevent involuntary node loss or every deletion path. Controllers performing rolling upgrades also have their own availability settings; a PDB is not a universal rollout governor.

concepts.name: Eviction versus deletion
concepts.body: Draining normally cordons a node and requests eviction of suitable workloads. Eviction respects applicable budget decisions, while direct deletion can bypass that protection. DaemonSets, unmanaged Pods, local data, and termination behavior require deliberate handling rather than blindly adding force or deletion flags.

concepts.name: Replacement readiness
concepts.body: Maintenance depends on replacements becoming available somewhere else. A cluster with no spare capacity or restrictive affinity can deadlock a drain even when the application is healthy. Readiness checks must represent actual service ability; otherwise the budget may count unusable capacity as healthy.

concepts.name: Upgrade sequencing
concepts.body: A safe upgrade checks version compatibility, backups, dependencies, and rollback limits before moving through small batches. Node and control-plane upgrades differ. Observe service indicators after each batch and stop when recovery fails instead of treating successful infrastructure operations as proof of application health.

e2e: Preflight checks confirm compatibility, restore options, and spare schedulable capacity.
A node is cordoned so new ordinary Pods do not land there.
Evictions proceed only within allowed disruption and termination constraints.
Replacements become ready elsewhere; service checks pass before the next maintenance batch.

tasks.name: Calculate allowed disruption
steps: Five healthy selected replicas with minAvailable=4 permit one voluntary disruption initially. After one becomes unavailable, another eviction must wait until health returns. If an unrelated node failure removes a second replica, the budget cannot undo that involuntary loss and permits no further voluntary disruption.

tasks.name: Find a drain deadlock
steps: Model three replicas with minAvailable=2, each pinned to a different node, and no free destination capacity. Evict one on paper and show its replacement Pending. Explain why lowering minAvailable may worsen availability rather than create any new schedulable capacity.

tasks.name: Design termination checks
steps: Write a timeline including readiness removal, endpoint propagation, graceful application stop, and a bounded termination grace period. Identify evidence that long-running requests finished. Avoid assuming a Pod disappearing from a list means its user transactions completed successfully.

tasks.name: Create an upgrade gate
tasks.goal: Define an objective maintenance stop rule.
steps: For a fictional checkout service, require healthy replacement count, stable error ratio, and a completed synthetic transaction before the next node. Include a compatibility check for API removals and storage drivers. Explain when rollback is unsupported and restore or forward repair must be planned instead.

key_terms: PDB: selected voluntary-disruption availability budget.
Cordon: mark a node unschedulable.
Drain: evacuate eligible node workloads.
Eviction: API-mediated request for Pod removal.
lesson.safety: Do not drain shared nodes or bypass disruption protections; perform only offline maintenance planning.
cleanup: Discard the fictional upgrade checklist; no cluster state changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a node drain stalls behind a disruption budget. What do you investigate before changing the budget?
interview_points: Check healthy counts, readiness, and in-progress disruptions.
Inspect replacement scheduling and spare capacity.
Avoid force deletion and define application-level stop gates.

storyboard.title: Maintenance waits for replacement health
storyboard.objective: Show why a blocked drain may protect availability.

scenes.title: Evict within budget
scenes.caption: One disruption is allowed.
scenes.narration: The first eviction proceeds while the required healthy count remains protected.

scenes.title: Replacement waits
scenes.caption: No capacity means no recovery.
scenes.narration: The replacement cannot schedule, so further voluntary evictions remain blocked.

scenes.title: Restore available capacity
scenes.caption: Health unlocks the next batch.
scenes.narration: After compatible capacity becomes ready, the replacement recovers and maintenance can continue.

kubernetes/kubernetes-disruption-budgets.core: PDBs constrain voluntary eviction, not all outages or deletion paths. Drain safety requires spare capacity, truthful readiness, graceful termination, and application-level upgrade gates.

lesson.title: Kubernetes jobs CronJobs and operators
lesson.why: Background automation must tolerate retries and interrupted execution. A successful scheduler event does not prove exactly one business effect occurred.
lesson.what: Compare bounded batch Jobs, time-based CronJobs, and continuously reconciling operators using an idempotent reporting example.

concepts.name: Job completion
concepts.body: A Job creates Pods until its completion criteria are met, subject to retry and deadline controls. Parallelism controls concurrent execution rather than an exactly-once guarantee. A process can complete an external write and then fail before Kubernetes observes success, causing a retry of the same business work.

concepts.name: CronJob schedules
concepts.body: A CronJob creates Jobs according to a schedule and supported time-zone configuration. Concurrency policies govern overlapping Jobs from that CronJob, not unrelated workloads. Scheduling can be delayed or missed, so business logic should handle duplicate or absent execution instead of treating clock ticks as durable transactions.

concepts.name: Idempotent effects
concepts.body: An idempotency key identifies the logical operation independently of a Pod attempt. Store completion atomically with the business effect where possible, or use deduplication and reconciliation. A lock alone is insufficient if the process crashes after the effect but before recording completion.

concepts.name: Operator control loops
concepts.body: Operators extend reconciliation through custom resources and domain-specific controllers. They observe actual state and act repeatedly toward a desired state. Finalizers coordinate cleanup before deletion completes, but stuck finalizers require diagnosis; removing them without understanding external resources can leak data or infrastructure.

e2e: A schedule or user request defines one logical reporting period.
A Job starts a Pod carrying a stable period-based idempotency key.
Retries repeat execution safely because committed work is detected and not duplicated.
An operator can reconcile longer-lived dependencies and report status until desired state is reached.

tasks.name: Calculate concurrent work
steps: A Job requires six successful completions with parallelism two. With equal ten-second tasks and no retries or overhead, it needs three waves and thirty seconds. One failed attempt adds work but does not count as a successful completion; the ideal duration is therefore not a guarantee.

tasks.name: Design a reporting key
steps: Use the synthetic key report:2026-09-29 for a daily report. Model an attempt that writes its output and crashes before exit. On retry, check a transactionally recorded key and return the stored result rather than sending the report twice. Describe the atomicity requirement explicitly.

tasks.name: Choose overlap behavior
steps: A report starts every ten minutes but runs for fifteen. Compare Allow, Forbid, and Replace on a timeline. Explain which choice fits a noninterruptible export and why skipped or replaced work needs business-level reconciliation rather than simply counting created Jobs.

tasks.name: Diagnose operator deletion
steps: A fictional database custom resource remains terminating because snapshot cleanup fails. Identify the controller status, events, and external cleanup state needed before intervention. Propose repair and reconciliation first; describe the orphaning risk of manually removing a finalizer without completing its contract.

key_terms: Job: controller for finite task completion.
CronJob: schedule-driven Job creator.
Idempotency key: stable logical operation identifier.
Finalizer: deletion-blocking cleanup coordination marker.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic reports; do not schedule real mail, payments, or external cleanup operations.
cleanup: Discard the timeline; no Jobs, custom resources, or schedules were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a CronJob sends the same report twice after a Pod failure. How would you prevent duplicate business effects?
interview_points: Use a stable period-based key across retries.
Record the effect and deduplication state atomically.
Treat concurrency policy as scheduling control, not exactly-once delivery.

storyboard.title: A retry is not a new business operation
storyboard.objective: Separate Pod attempts from durable effects.

scenes.title: Commit report
scenes.caption: The business effect precedes process exit.
scenes.narration: The attempt records a period-keyed report before Kubernetes observes successful completion.

scenes.title: Attempt crashes
scenes.caption: A retry can repeat the code.
scenes.narration: The process fails after committing, so the Job controller starts another attempt.

scenes.title: Deduplicate retry
scenes.caption: The logical operation already completed.
scenes.narration: The next attempt finds the committed key and returns the stored result without resending.

kubernetes/kubernetes-jobs-cronjobs-and-.core: Jobs and CronJobs can retry or overlap; exactly-once business effects require application design. Operators reconcile custom resources repeatedly, and finalizers represent real cleanup obligations.

lesson.title: Kubernetes troubleshooting events logs and ephemeral containers
lesson.why: Changing a broken workload before collecting evidence can erase the best explanation. A staged investigation minimizes disruption and avoids leaking application data.
lesson.what: Use status, events, current and previous logs, and tightly scoped debugging access to distinguish scheduling, startup, and runtime problems.

concepts.name: State before intervention
concepts.body: Pod phase is a broad summary, not a complete diagnosis. Conditions, container states, restart counts, and termination reasons identify the failed stage. A Pending Pod may be unscheduled or waiting on setup after binding, while a Running Pod can contain an unhealthy application.

concepts.name: Events explain transitions
concepts.body: Events often reveal scheduling conflicts, image pull failures, and mount problems. They are time-limited operational observations, not a complete durable audit trail. Correlate timestamps and object identity because a replacement Pod with the same application label is not the same execution instance.

concepts.name: Logs need context
concepts.body: Container logs explain application behavior; previous-instance logs can help after a restart. Select the intended container in multi-container Pods and correlate requests without exposing tokens or personal data. Absence of logs can reflect failure before process startup rather than a logging outage.

concepts.name: Ephemeral debugging
concepts.body: Ephemeral containers can add debugging tools to an existing Pod when permitted, including images lacking shells. They do not restart the original container and are not removed individually like a normal process cleanup. Namespace visibility and capabilities depend on configuration; privilege must be explicitly justified.

e2e: Capture the failing Pod identity, time window, phase, conditions, and restart evidence.
Use events to locate scheduling, image, volume, or health-check transitions.
Read the relevant current or previous container logs within that time window.
Escalate to approved debugging only when simpler evidence cannot test the remaining hypothesis.

tasks.name: Classify a timeline
tasks.goal: Choose the first useful evidence source.
steps: At 10:00 a Pod is bound, at 10:01 image pulls fail, and at 10:02 no application logs exist. Conclude that startup never reached the application. Inspect image reference, registry reachability, and pull authorization rather than inventing an application stack trace.

tasks.name: Work a restart calculation
steps: A synthetic restart count rises from 4 to 7 during a fifteen-minute observation. The interval contains three restarts, averaging one every five minutes. The count alone does not prove periodic behavior; request exact termination times and reasons before diagnosing a scheduled failure.

tasks.name: Plan read-only commands
steps: For an authorized disposable context, draft kubectl describe pod demo -n lesson and kubectl logs demo -n lesson -c app --previous --tail=50. Do not execute against a shared context. Explain why --previous fails when no previous container instance exists and why output may need redaction.

tasks.name: Justify deeper inspection
steps: A shell-less image reports DNS timeouts after startup. List resolver settings, Service endpoints, and policy evidence before requesting an ephemeral container. Specify approved tools, minimum capabilities, and an exit plan; record that the ephemeral-container entry remains until the Pod is replaced.

key_terms: Condition: detailed lifecycle status signal.
Event: time-limited object transition observation.
Previous logs: output from a terminated container instance.
Ephemeral container: debugging container added to an existing Pod.
lesson.safety: Do not collect real credentials or add debug containers without authorization; default exercises are offline.
cleanup: Discard synthetic evidence; any real approved debug Pod replacement needs its normal owner-controlled rollout.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a shell-less Pod repeatedly restarts. What evidence would you collect before adding a debug container?
interview_points: Capture identity, conditions, termination reasons, and timing.
Inspect previous logs and relevant events first.
Limit debugging privileges and account for persistent Pod metadata.

storyboard.title: Evidence narrows the failed lifecycle stage

scenes.title: Capture state
scenes.caption: Preserve identity before intervention.
scenes.narration: The investigator records the Pod identity and container termination state.

scenes.title: Find the failed handoff
scenes.caption: No logs may mean no process started.
scenes.narration: Image pull events show that the application never reached execution.

scenes.title: Repair the demonstrated cause
scenes.caption: Debug only what remains unexplained.
scenes.narration: Correcting the image access problem allows startup without adding unnecessary privileged tools.

kubernetes/kubernetes-troubleshooting-ev.core: Start with identity, conditions, events, and prior logs. Escalate to ephemeral debugging only for a specific unresolved hypothesis, with bounded privileges and explicit lifecycle expectations.

lesson.title: Kubernetes multi-cluster backup and disaster recovery
lesson.why: A second cluster is not a recovery plan unless workloads, data, identity, and traffic can move consistently. Replicated mistakes can destroy both copies.
lesson.what: Separate cluster configuration recovery from application data recovery and build an offline failover sequence with explicit RPO and RTO accounting.

concepts.name: Recovery inventory
concepts.body: Git may reconstruct manifests but not every Secret, persistent volume, external database, custom resource, or controller dependency. An etcd snapshot protects control-plane state within supported restore procedures, not arbitrary external storage contents. Inventory each state owner and its independent recovery mechanism.

concepts.name: Recovery objectives
concepts.body: Recovery point objective bounds acceptable data loss, while recovery time objective bounds time to restore useful service. Snapshot frequency alone does not establish either result. Backup completion, log replay, validation, credential recovery, and traffic switching all contribute to the achieved outcome.

concepts.name: Multi-cluster dependencies
concepts.body: Clusters can share failure domains through identity providers, registries, DNS, or regional storage. Replicating Kubernetes objects across clusters does not make volume formats portable. Version compatibility, installed CRDs, admission policies, and controller ordering must be verified before restoring dependent resources.

concepts.name: Safe failover
concepts.body: Promoting a replacement writer requires fencing or otherwise preventing the old writer from accepting conflicting writes. Traffic migration and data promotion need a coordinated runbook. Failback is another migration with reconciliation and verification, not simply changing DNS back after the original cluster returns.

e2e: Inventory critical configuration, data, identity, and external service recovery dependencies.
Create protected backups and verify restore access in an isolated target.
Restore compatible controllers and data, then validate integrity and application health.
Fence the old writer, move traffic, measure service recovery, and plan controlled failback.

tasks.name: Calculate recovery gaps
steps: An incident occurs at 14:20; the latest recoverable consistent point is 14:05. Potential data loss is fifteen minutes. Detection takes five minutes, restoration twenty, validation ten, and cutover five: sequential recovery totals forty minutes. A ten-minute RPO or thirty-minute RTO is therefore missed.

tasks.name: Build a backup inventory
steps: List Deployment manifests, encrypted secret material, database records, volume snapshots, CRDs, and registry images for a fictional ledger service. Assign each an owner and restore source. Explain why restoring Deployments before their required CRDs or data can produce misleading partial success.

tasks.name: Diagnose shared failure
steps: Assume two clusters use the same regional identity endpoint and image registry. Model an outage of that region and identify which recovery steps stall. Propose independently accessible recovery artifacts and authentication while documenting the added governance and consistency burden.

tasks.name: Practice fenced promotion
steps: Write a failover checklist that verifies backup integrity, blocks the old writer, promotes one target, tests a synthetic record, and changes traffic. Include an abort rule if fencing cannot be proven. Define how returning writes are reconciled before any failback is attempted.

key_terms: RPO: acceptable recovery-point data loss.
RTO: acceptable service recovery duration.
Fencing: preventing conflicting writer activity.
Restore drill: controlled proof of recoverability.
lesson.safety: Use fictional incidents; never promote a live replica, restore over source data, or change real DNS.
cleanup: Discard the drill timeline; no backups or clusters were altered.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, manifests restore successfully in another cluster but the service cannot recover. What dependencies might the plan have missed?
interview_points: Separate control-plane objects from persistent and external data.
Check CRDs, identity, registry, encryption keys, and topology.
Validate recovery objectives and prevent concurrent writers.

storyboard.title: A second cluster needs recoverable state
storyboard.objective: Separate manifests, data restore, and safe promotion.

scenes.title: Capture recoverable state
scenes.caption: Configuration alone is insufficient.
scenes.narration: Protected data and configuration backups establish a known recovery point.

scenes.title: Original cluster fails
scenes.caption: Recovery begins from the available point.
scenes.narration: The target must restore dependencies and data before it can safely serve writes.

scenes.title: Validate and promote
scenes.caption: Fence before switching writers.
scenes.narration: After integrity checks and fencing, the recovery cluster can accept controlled traffic.

kubernetes/kubernetes-multi-cluster-back.core: Multi-cluster recovery requires independent configuration, data, identity, and artifact recovery. Measure actual RPO/RTO, restore dependencies in order, and fence old writers before promotion.
